name: Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues

clinicalPearls: An anatomic approach is the key to diagnosis: the level and physical appearance of the lesion (epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, fascia, or muscle) together with location, time course, travel/animal-bite history, age, comorbidities, and lifestyle narrow the differential (Harrison 22e p.1049-1052).

Because the avascular epidermis is protected mainly by the stratum corneum, any breach (burns, bites, abrasions, foreign bodies, ulcers, surgery, primary dermatologic disease) lets bacteria reach deeper structures (Harrison 22e p.1049).

Edema with purple bullae, ecchymosis, and cutaneous anesthesia signals loss of vascular integrity and mandates exploration of deep structures for necrotizing fasciitis or myonecrosis (Harrison 22e p.1049).

Unexplained fever plus disproportionate soft-tissue pain and tenderness, even without overt cutaneous inflammation, should raise high suspicion for a deep necrotizing infection and prompt early diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1049).

Vesicular lesions reflect viral proliferation within the epidermis (e.g., varicella with crops of 'dewdrop' vesicles, dermatomal herpes zoster preceded by pain, HSV around lips or genitals, coxsackievirus A16 hand-foot-mouth); rickettsialpox produces a crusted black eschar after mite-bite inoculation of Rickettsia akari (Harrison 22e p.1049-1050).

Crusted golden-brown lesions suggest impetigo: impetigo contagiosa from S. pyogenes (linked to poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but NOT rheumatic fever) and bullous impetigo from S. aureus; MRSA impetigo epidemics have been reported (Harrison 22e p.1051).

A focused exposure history points to the organism in cellulitis: cat/dog bites (Pasteurella multocida, also S. intermedius, Capnocytophaga), freshwater lacerations (Aeromonas hydrophila), Gulf of Mexico/Atlantic saltwater or raw seafood in cirrhosis (Vibrio vulnificus), fish/swine handling (Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae), and aquariums/swimming pools (Mycobacterium marinum) (Harrison 22e p.1050-1052).

Cultures are frequently unrevealing in cellulitis: even needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy is positive in only about 20% of cases, suggesting low bacterial numbers and a toxin/inflammatory-mediator effect (Harrison 22e p.1052).

Erysipelas (S. pyogenes) shows abrupt fiery-red swelling with sharply demarcated indurated margins (classically along the nasolabial fold), rapid spread, and intense pain; desquamation follows at 5-10 days (Harrison 22e p.1052).

Imaging (plain films, CT, MRI) helps localize abscess or detect gas in tissue but may show only nonspecific soft-tissue swelling; notably, gas is usually absent in necrotizing fasciitis and myonecrosis caused by group A Streptococcus or MRSA, so a negative gas finding does not exclude fulminant infection (Harrison 22e p.1053).
Hospital admissions for skin and soft tissue infections rose ~27% from 2000-2004, largely due to emergence of the USA300 MRSA clone (Harrison 22e p.1049).

Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus, common in the tropics) typically has no portal of entry and begins at the exact site of blunt trauma or muscle strain; PVL-producing MRSA pyomyositis has occurred in U.S. children (Harrison 22e p.1053).
harrison.pathophysiology: Infection localizes according to skin anatomy. The epidermis is avascular and relies on the stratum corneum as a mechanical barrier; disruption permits bacterial entry, and hair follicles act as portals for normal flora (Staphylococcus) or exogenous organisms (Pseudomonas in hot-tub folliculitis). The rich subpapillary capillary plexus mediates inflammatory signs and allows metastatic seeding (Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, palpable purpura in endocarditis; cutaneous lesions of disseminated fungal, gonococcal, Salmonella, Pseudomonas/ecthyma gangrenosum, meningococcal, and staphylococcal infection) and access to the bloodstream. Bacteria such as S. pyogenes spread laterally via lymphatics, producing rapidly extending erysipelas, and subsequent lymphatic obstruction causes flaccid epidermal edema. Excess cytokines or bacterial toxins amplify these responses, causing leukostasis, venous occlusion, and edema; loss of vascular integrity produces purple bullae and cutaneous anesthesia indicative of deep necrotizing infection. In necrotizing fasciitis, infection extends along fascial planes and through venous channels and lymphatics, with dermal-papillary vessel thrombosis and progression to friable, bluish/black skin and systemic toxicity. Group A streptococcal and clostridial muscle infection can produce acute rhabdomyolysis with markedly elevated creatine phosphokinase. Toxin biology drives several syndromes: exfoliatin (phage group II S. aureus) cleaves the stratum corneum in staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, while PVL-producing MRSA can cause necrotizing fasciitis and pyomyositis, and TSST-1/enterotoxins underlie shock in toxic shock syndrome (Harrison 22e p.1049-1053).
additionalDifferentials: Vesicular: varicella, herpes zoster, HSV-1/HSV-2, hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackievirus A16), orf, molluscum contagiosum, rickettsialpox, blistering distal dactylitis, smallpox/mpox
Bullous: staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene, halophilic Vibrio (V. vulnificus)
Crusted: impetigo contagiosa/bullous impetigo, ringworm (dermatophytes), sporotrichosis, blastomycosis, disseminated coccidioidomycosis, cutaneous TB, M. chelonae nodules in HIV

Papulonodular: M. marinum, cat-scratch disease/bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae), cutaneous larva migrans, dracunculiasis, onchocerciasis, verruga peruana (B. bacilliformis), cysticercosis, lepromatous leprosy, secondary/tertiary syphilis, HPV warts
Ulcers/eschars: cutaneous anthrax, ulceroglandular tularemia, bubonic plague, Buruli ulcer (M. ulcerans), leprosy, cutaneous TB, chancroid, primary syphilis
infectionMimics: Sebaceous cysts blocked at the follicular duct can resemble or become secondarily infected like staphylococcal abscesses
Hidradenitis suppurativa (sweat-gland inflammation, especially axillary) can mimic hair-follicle infection
Crusted primary infections with Blastomyces dermatitidis or Sporothrix schenckii can initially resemble ringworm
nonInfectiousMimics: Toxic epidermal necrolysis (drug-induced, adult, higher mortality) versus staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome; distinguished by frozen-section cleavage plane (stratum germinativum in TEN vs stratum corneum in SSSS)
Pyoderma gangrenosum on the anterior shins, distinguished from infectious ulcers by biopsy histology
Decubitus (pressure) ulcers from pressure-induced vascular insufficiency, which may become secondarily infected
Early necrotizing fasciitis misdiagnosed as thrombophlebitis or a simple muscle strain/bruise
additionalInvestigations: Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or obvious portal of entry give a definitive cellulitis diagnosis when present
Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy (positive in only ~20% of cellulitis and ~80% negative in deep infections)
Punch biopsy with frozen section to distinguish SSSS from TEN and to evaluate necrotizing fasciitis
KOH staining of skin scrapings for dermatophyte (ringworm) infection
Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth, localize abscess, and detect tissue gas
Serum creatine phosphokinase, which may be markedly elevated in concomitant myositis/myonecrosis
Open surgical inspection with debridement as the best means of determining extent/severity and obtaining material for Gram stain and culture
Biopsy and culture of crusted lesions in patients from endemic areas (e.g., for Coccidioides immitis)
redFlags: Disproportionate pain and tenderness with unexplained fever and minimal skin findings
Edema with purple/violaceous bullae, ecchymosis, skin sloughing, or cutaneous anesthesia
Rapidly progressing lesion with brawny edema, dark-red or bluish/maroon/black skin discoloration
Systemic toxicity, shock, multiorgan failure, or renal impairment preceding shock (streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis/TSS)
Scrotal/perineal swelling extending to abdominal wall or legs (Fournier gangrene)

Postpartum or post-abortion woman with little/no fever, no purulent discharge, refractory hypotension, marked edema/effusions, hemoconcentration, and a very high WBC count (Clostridium sordellii infection - often rapidly fatal)
Halophilic Vibrio infection that is as fulminant as necrotizing fasciitis with seawater/raw-seafood exposure, especially in cirrhosis
harrison.prognosis: Outcome ranges from benign and self-limited (e.g., hot-tub folliculitis, though rare bacteremia and shock have occurred) to rapidly fatal. Necrotizing fasciitis with no defined portal of entry carries high mortality, and survivors often require repeated surgery including amputation. Clostridium sordellii infection (postpartum, post-abortion, or black-tar-heroin injection) is often fatal with rapid death. Mpox case-fatality (1-10%) is lower than smallpox, and TEN carries higher mortality than SSSS. Delay in surgical debridement significantly increases mortality in fulminant infections (Harrison 22e p.1050-1053).
pitfalls: Relying on absence of gas to exclude necrotizing fasciitis/myonecrosis - gas is usually absent with group A Streptococcus or MRSA
Sending home patients with severe pain and fever after misdiagnosing early necrotizing fasciitis as thrombophlebitis and giving only analgesia
Trusting negative imaging or biopsy (negative in ~80% of deep infections) to rule out fulminant infection
Using empirical vancomycin against Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, which is unusually vancomycin-resistant among gram-positive organisms
Confusing SSSS with TEN without frozen-section evaluation of the cleavage plane
Letting hyperbaric oxygen delay or substitute for surgical debridement when debridement is indicated
harrison.severityClassification: Clinically stratified by depth and aggressiveness rather than a single formal score: (1) superficial epidermal/follicular infections (vesicular, crusted, folliculitis); (2) dermal/lymphatic spread (erysipelas, cellulitis - subdivided into purulent cellulitis [MSSA/MRSA, focal abscess source] versus nonpurulent cellulitis [S. pyogenes, rapidly spreading, lymphangitis/fever]); and (3) deep, life-threatening necrotizing infections of fascia and muscle (necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene/myonecrosis, pyomyositis), signaled by systemic inflammatory response, shock, and multiorgan failure (Harrison 22e p.1052-1053).
